title: Sigma rule parser and intermediate representation
description: Parse the Sigma specification subset we support into a typed intermediate representation, rejecting anything outside that subset loudly rather than silently mis-evaluating it.
acceptance: Supports selection, condition, modifiers (contains, startswith, endswith, re, all, base64), and near/aggregation detection for routing to the windowed engine
An unsupported construct fails the build with a clear message naming the rule and the construct
The pinned Sigma specification version is recorded in config
Field names are mapped to OCSF paths through an explicit, reviewable mapping table
Parse errors identify the file, line and construct

tests.desc: Parses every rule in the committed corpus without error
Unsupported construct produces a precise, actionable error
Each supported modifier produces the expected intermediate representation
Field mapping failure for an unknown field is an error, not a silent no-match

title: Sigma-to-Go code generator
description: Implements ADR-0004. Emits compiled Go predicates plus a per-rule generated test built from that rule's fixtures.
acceptance: Generated code compiles and is committed, clearly marked as generated
A test is generated per rule asserting its positive fixture fires and its negative fixture does not
Compilation fails if a rule lacks a MITRE technique id
Compilation fails if a rule lacks either fixture
Regenerating produces no diff when inputs are unchanged

tests.desc: Generated matcher output equals a reference interpreter on a 10,000-event corpus
A rule without a MITRE id fails the build
A rule without a negative fixture fails the build
CI regeneration is diff-free for unchanged inputs

title: Field-indexed dispatch tree for rule evaluation
description: Rather than evaluating 150 rules per event, dispatch on high-selectivity fields first so a typical event is tested against a handful of candidates.
acceptance: Dispatch keys on class_uid, activity_id and metadata.product before rule-specific predicates
Candidate rule count per event is exported as a metric
Evaluation result is provably identical to exhaustive evaluation
Per-event evaluation stays under 50 microseconds at p99 on the reference corpus
Adding a rule does not require hand-editing the dispatch tree

tests.desc: Dispatch result is identical to exhaustive evaluation across the full fixture corpus
p99 per-event evaluation under 50 microseconds with 150 rules loaded
A rule matching on a low-selectivity field is still reached correctly

title: In-stream detection worker
description: Consumes normalised events, evaluates compiled rules, and emits Signals to the signals topic with full event references attached.
acceptance: Every emitted signal references the event_id that produced it
Signals carry rule id, MITRE technique, severity and tenant
Consumer lag is exported per partition
Evaluation errors route to DLQ without halting the worker
Horizontal scaling is linear up to the partition count

tests.desc: A known malicious event sequence produces exactly the expected signal set
A worker crash mid-batch replays without losing signals
30k EPS sustained across a scaled worker set
An evaluation panic is recovered, routed to DLQ, and the worker continues

title: Windowed detection rules executing in ClickHouse
description: Stateful rules that need a join against history — impossible travel, brute force, mass download, baseline deviation — as scheduled parameterised ClickHouse queries.
acceptance: Rule class determines schedule: 30s for high-urgency, up to 15 minutes for baseline rules
Queries are parameterised and tenant-scoped; no string interpolation of tenant identifiers
Overlapping executions are prevented by a per-rule lock
A rule exceeding its time budget is killed and alerted on rather than left running
Results emit signals on the same topic and in the same shape as in-stream rules

tests.desc: Impossible travel fires for a seeded two-country sign-in pair inside the velocity threshold
Impossible travel does not fire for legitimate VPN-shaped travel in the negative fixture
Query parameterisation resists an injection attempt via tenant-controlled input
A long-running query is killed at its budget and raises an alert

title: The first 40 detection rules with fixtures
description: The 40 rules that matter for small-business M365 compromise. Chosen by what actually happens, not by what is easy to detect.
acceptance: 40 rules covering: impossible travel, external inbox forwarding rule, mass mailbox download, OAuth consent to unverified app, MFA method registration anomaly, anonymous proxy sign-in, mass file download or delete, privileged role assignment, password spray, legacy auth usage, mailbox audit disabled, and inbox rule hiding messages
Every rule has a positive and a negative fixture derived from realistic event shapes
Every rule is mapped to a MITRE ATT&CK technique
Every rule has a plain-English description written for a non-technical owner
Measured false-positive rate under 20% on the replayed reference dataset

tests.desc: All 40 positive fixtures fire their intended rule
All 40 negative fixtures fire nothing
Replay of a benign reference week produces a false-positive rate under 20%
Every rule description is present and contains no unexplained jargon, checked by a term allowlist

title: MITRE ATT&CK mapping and enforcement
description: Technique ids validated against the published ATT&CK catalogue, with coverage reporting so gaps are visible rather than assumed.
acceptance: Technique ids are validated against a pinned ATT&CK version at build time
An invalid or retired technique id fails the build
A coverage report shows which tactics and techniques are and are not covered
Coverage is rendered as a navigator-compatible layer for stakeholders
Technique metadata is available to the AI analyst and the customer-facing report

tests.desc: An invalid technique id fails the build
Coverage report counts match the rule corpus
Generated navigator layer loads without error in the ATT&CK Navigator

title: Critical-alert bypass path
description: Rules marked critical publish directly to the alert channel in parallel with entering correlation, so a detection reaches the customer even if correlation and the AI analyst are entirely down.
acceptance: Critical signals publish to the alert path in parallel with the correlation path
The bypass has no dependency on correlation, the analyst, or the LLM provider
The bypass alert is clearly labelled as rule-generated rather than AI-investigated
Deduplication prevents the customer receiving both a bypass alert and an AI alert for the same case
The bypass path is exercised by a scheduled synthetic test in production

tests.desc: Chaos test: analyst service killed, critical alert still delivered within SLA
Chaos test: correlation service killed, critical alert still delivered
LLM provider returning 503 does not prevent critical alert delivery
Customer receives exactly one notification when both paths complete successfully

title: Threat intelligence enrichment
description: IP reputation, anonymiser and hosting-provider classification, and geolocation, cached locally so detection never blocks on a third-party lookup.
acceptance: Feeds are refreshed on a schedule and cached locally; detection never makes a synchronous external call
Geolocation and ASN are attached to every sign-in event at enrichment time
Anonymiser, VPN and hosting-provider classification is available as a rule predicate
A stale feed degrades gracefully and raises an operational alert
Indicator provenance is recorded so a report can cite which feed flagged an address

tests.desc: Known Tor exit node is classified as an anonymiser
Geolocation enrichment is correct for a known address set
Feed provider outage does not stall detection
Stale feed beyond its threshold raises an alert

title: Detection tuning, suppression and allowlisting
description: Per-tenant suppression of known-benign patterns, with every suppression recorded and visible. Suppression must never become an invisible hole in coverage.
acceptance: Suppressions are scoped to a tenant, a rule and an entity or pattern
Every suppression records who created it, when and why
Suppressed signals are still stored and counted, just not escalated
Suppressions expire by default and require explicit renewal
The dashboard shows active suppressions and what they have suppressed

tests.desc: A suppressed signal is stored but not escalated
An expired suppression stops suppressing
A suppression in one tenant has no effect in another
Creating a suppression without a reason is rejected

title: Detection engine load test at 30k EPS
description: The P2 exit criterion as an executable, repeatable load test with a CI-enforced regression gate.
acceptance: k6 or equivalent harness generates a realistic 30k EPS mixed event stream
Runs for one hour with stable memory and no goroutine leak
Detection latency p99 stays under 100 milliseconds
Results are recorded and a regression beyond 10% fails the build
The harness is runnable locally at reduced scale

tests.desc: 30k EPS sustained for one hour with p99 under 100ms
Memory stable across the run with no leak
A deliberately introduced 20% regression fails the gate

title: Emergency hotfix rule path
description: The escape hatch named in ADR-0004: a small interpreted rule path for urgent detections, deliberately constrained so it cannot become the normal way rules are added.
acceptance: Maximum 10 active hotfix rules platform-wide
Each expires automatically after 7 days with no option to extend in place
Creating one requires an elevated role and writes an audit entry
Active hotfix rules are listed on the operations dashboard with their expiry
Expiry notification prompts proper compilation of the rule

tests.desc: An 11th hotfix rule is rejected
A hotfix rule stops evaluating after 7 days
Creation by a non-elevated role is denied and audited

title: Detection engineering guide
description: How to write, map, fixture and tune a rule, written so a new detection engineer can ship their first rule without reading the compiler.
acceptance: Covers rule authoring, MITRE mapping, fixture construction and the tuning workflow
Explains why negative fixtures are mandatory, with a concrete example of the failure they prevent
Includes a worked end-to-end example of adding one rule
Documents the supported Sigma subset and what to do when a rule needs more

tests.desc: A new engineer ships a working rule following only the guide
